1.Nc3.name: Dunst Opening
1.Nc3.background: Named after Ted A. Dunst (1907–1985), a New York master; in the Netherlands called the Van Geet Opening after Dick van Geet (1932–2012), who played it frequently. Its recorded origin is Blackburne against Noa, London 1883.

1.Nc3 d5.strategy: The principal reply: Black takes the centre and threatens to push the pawn to d4, which would hit the knight and win space. White's knight is also in the way of its own c-pawn, so White has to decide at once whether to allow that or prevent it.

1.Nc3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 from the wing and leaves the centre flexible. If White answers with e4, the knight on c3 blocks its own c-pawn and takes some sting out of White's set-up, so Black faces few problems.

1.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: A patient developing move that hands the decision about the centre back to White. Black keeps both a classical central set-up and a fianchetto open, and White has no obvious way to claim a real advantage.

1.Nc3 e5.name: Dunst Opening: Reversed Nimzowitsch
1.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and invites White to develop with tempo against the e5 pawn. Playable, but it leaves White a slight lasting initiative, and Black has to know the tactical traps that White's knights can set.

1.Nc3 d6.strategy: A modest, flexible move that prepares to meet the centre with ...e5 or a developing knight later. It claims no space now, so White can build a broad pawn centre without being challenged at once.

1.Nc3 f5.strategy: Contests e4 in the manner of a Dutch Defence, but White's knight already watches that square, so the move gains less than against other first moves and loosens Black's kingside. White simply claims the centre with a pawn.

1.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto: Black controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. Reasonable, but it leaves White free to take the centre with pawns first, and Black has to prove later that the space is not a burden.

1.Nc3 b5.name: Dunst Opening: Laroche Gambit
1.Nc3 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for a lead in development, but the knight just takes it, and Black has little to show for the pawn beyond a bishop on the long diagonal. A dubious gambit that gives White an easy extra pawn.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once and offers a pawn trade that brings White's queen out early. It surprises Black, but the queen becomes a target for Black's development, so White gains little more than a sharp start.

1.Nc3 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and prepares to open the centre with a pawn, keeping White's choices flexible. Black can still stake a claim in the centre at once, so White gets a pleasant but not a commanding game.

1.Nc3 c5 2.Rb1.name: Dunst Opening: Twyble Attack
1.Nc3 c5 2.Rb1.strategy: Prepares to advance the b-pawn for queenside space without exposing the rook, but it develops nothing and spends a tempo on a rook move. Harmless rather than bad: Black simply uses the time to take the centre.

1.Nc3 c5 2.b4.name: Dunst Opening: Düsseldorf Gambit
1.Nc3 c5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to open the b-file and drag Black's c-pawn away, but Black takes it with ...cxb4 and attacks the knight with the pawn at the same time. White has no clear compensation for the lost pawn and the lost time.

1.Nc3 c5 2.e4.strategy: The natural continuation: White claims central space with the e-pawn and keeps the d-pawn back, heading for a calm game of piece development and a later kingside pawn advance. It avoids sharp open lines and keeps the knight on its good square, a sound way to play on.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn. Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, which removes White's only advanced central pawn and leaves Black a half-open c-file to play on.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and presses on e4 and d5, but it leaves the tension in the centre: White can win a pawn with dxc5, which Black must then win back, or gain space with d5. Playable, but more passive than taking on d4.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 e6.strategy: Solid: the pawn prepares ...d5 and opens the bishop, so dxc5 can be answered by taking the pawn straight back. But it leaves White to decide what happens to the tension in the centre, so Black gets a sound but slightly passive game.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: The natural recapture: the queen lands in the middle of the board and White's pawn structure stays intact. The price is an early queen that Black can harass with developing moves, so White has to play for activity.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn with a piece instead of recapturing, but Black simply defends it with ...e5 and keeps the extra pawn. White has only a lead in development to show for it, so this gives a pawn away rather than gaining time.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Nb5.strategy: Drops a piece: ...Qa5+ checks the king and attacks the knight at once, and every block leaves it lost, since 4.Nc3 runs into ...dxc3 and 4.Bd2 or 4.Qd2 allow ...Qxb5. White has no compensation for the lost piece.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with tempo: the knight attacks the queen, which has to leave the centre again. Black gets a piece out while White's queen is chased, and the tempo outweighs White's lead in the middle.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and eyes e4, so White has to support any advance of the e-pawn, while ...Nc6 can still chase the queen. A comfortable game, though it does not win the tempo that the knight on c6 does at once.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 d6.strategy: Solid: the pawn opens the queen's bishop and the queen's diagonal, but it does not touch the queen. White gets a free move to build the centre, and Black has a sound Sicilian-style structure without the initiative.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qh4.name: Dunst Opening: Novosibirsk Variation
1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qh4.background: Schiller calls the line the Novosibirsk Variation.
1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qh4.strategy: Moves the queen to a safe square where it eyes e7 and h7, but both are well defended, so nothing is threatened. It is a second queen move, so Black develops freely and takes the centre at once; White stays sound but a little behind.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1.strategy: Goes back to the starting square: the safest retreat, with every piece free to develop. The price is time, since the queen has moved twice and ends where it began, so Black is a tempo ahead and has the bigger share of the centre.

1.Nc3 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qa4.strategy: Moves to a4 and eyes the c6 knight, but two pawns defend it, so nothing is threatened. The queen stands far from the centre and the kingside, and Black develops and takes the middle while White spends time bringing it back into play.

1.Nc3 d5 2.e4.strategy: The usual choice: White claims the centre at once and accepts that Black may chase the knight with ...d4 for space. Whichever way Black answers, White keeps a flexible game.

1.Nc3 d5 2.e3.strategy: A quiet way to stop ...d4 and open the diagonal for the king's bishop. It is solid, but White gives up the immediate fight for the centre; the queen can come out to h5 later to harass an advanced e-pawn.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the queen's bishop and controls e4, but it does not stop ...d4 and gives up the d-pawn's claim on the centre. Solid and slow: White gives Black the first claim to the centre in return for a flexible set-up.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4.strategy: Takes e5 under control, but it does not stop ...d4 and loosens the diagonal to White's king. A committal move that gives Black an easy time in the centre.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and watches e4, so White cannot easily claim the centre with a pawn. Black holds the centre with pieces behind the d5 pawn and has a comfortable game.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn at once: White's slow d3 does not contest it, so Black gets a broad pawn centre and free development with nothing to attack. The centre needs some care, since a pawn that advances too early becomes a target.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 d4.strategy: Chases the knight and gains space, but it does not win a tempo: the knight has a good square on e4 and the pawn on d4 needs support. Black gets a cramping pawn that can become a target if White attacks it with pieces.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 Nf6 3.g3.name: Dunst Opening: Venezolana Variation
1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to put the bishop on the long diagonal, from where it pressures the d5 pawn and the centre. A slow, flexible set-up that avoids committing the e-pawn and aims for a quiet manoeuvring game.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible, natural move: the knight develops and controls d4 and e5 without fixing any pawn. White decides the structure later, after seeing how Black sets up, and gives Black no target.

1.Nc3 d5 2.d3 Nf6 3.e4.strategy: Strikes for the centre at once, but lets Black trade on e4 and exchange queens. White regains the pawn, yet the king has to recapture on d1 and loses the right to castle, for only a modest endgame.

1.Nc3 d5 2.e3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, but it invites a queen sortie to h5 that hits e5 and f7 together, so Black must develop with care. Playable, and Black keeps the more active pawn centre.

1.Nc3 d5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a purpose: the knight controls e4 and h5, which takes the sting out of a queen sortie to h5, and it commits Black to no pawn structure yet. A comfortable, solid game with no weakness to defend.

1.Nc3 d5 2.e3 c5.strategy: Hits the centre from the flank before White can build one and sets up an uneven pawn structure with queenside counterplay. It develops nothing and leaves d5 held only by the queen, so White has the easier development, but the position is balanced.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4.strategy: Chases the knight at once and wins space. With White's f-pawn already advanced, the king's side is loosened, the knight has to find a new square, and Black takes the initiative.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 e5.name: Dunst Opening: Damhaug Gambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 e5.strategy: A counter-strike in the centre: Black offers the e-pawn and opens the queen's diagonal towards White's king, which the f4 pawn has already left exposed. A double-edged gambit that asks White to keep its nerve.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 g5.name: Dunst Opening: Warsteiner Gambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 g5.strategy: Hits the f4 pawn at once, but White just takes it, and Black's kingside is left loosened with no clear return for the pawn. A dubious gambit that mainly weakens Black's own king.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and controls e4, so White cannot play e4 without losing a pawn, and keeps d5 firmly held. Black keeps its options open, and the advanced f-pawn already commits White's kingside, so Black has a comfortable, flexible game.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4.strategy: The natural retreat: the knight stays in the centre, where it eyes c5, d6, f6 and g5, and the f-pawn covers e5 and g5 beside it. The price is the space Black has gained with ...d4, and the knight can be driven off again, so White plays for activity rather than for the centre.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Nb1.strategy: Undoes 1.Nc3: the knight goes back to its starting square, White has spent two moves to get there and Black's pawn has gained space for free. The position is safe and the advanced pawn can be challenged later with a pawn break in the centre, but Black leads in space.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Nb5.strategy: Eyes c7 and d4, but the queen guards both, and ...c6 drives the knight back at once to a3. From there it can reach c4, so little is lost but time: the knight has moved three times while Black has gained space.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5.strategy: Drives the knight from its central post with a gain of time and claims e4, so together with the d4 pawn Black takes the space. The price is a loosened king's side: e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal stay weak for the rest of the game.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 c5.name: Dunst Opening: Melleby Gambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 c5.strategy: Offers the c-pawn for no clear return: the knight on e4 attacks it and nothing defends it, so White simply takes it. The knight can step back to safety afterwards, leaving Black a pawn down with only a modest lead in space.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5.name: Dunst Opening: Pfeiffer Gambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open the centre while White's king is still uncastled. White can take it with the f-pawn, and Black's compensation rests on gaining time against the knight on e4 and on open lines, which is thin for a pawn.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the undefended knight on e4 at once, while the d4 pawn keeps cramping White. Black gains time without loosening the king's side the way ...f5 does, so it is the sounder way to hold the space.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5 4.Nf3.name: Dunst Opening: Pfeiffer Gambit, Sleipnir Countergambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: Declines the free pawn: e5 is attacked twice, but White develops instead of taking, and Black wins a pawn with ...exf4. White must hope that quicker development and the d4 pawn, held only by the queen, bring enough play; simply capturing on e5 is the safer answer to the gambit.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5 4.fxe5.strategy: Accepts the gambit and makes Black prove its compensation. ...Qd5 hits the knight on e4 and the pawn on e5 together, so the pawn probably goes back, but White can then develop with tempo against the queen in an open position.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 e5 4.d3.strategy: Supports the knight with a pawn and opens the c1-bishop, so ...exf4 can be met by Bxf4. White keeps the knight in the centre and declines the pawn, but Black has more space and ...f5 chases the knight again.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2.strategy: The safest retreat: the knight covers e4, d3 and g4 and stays near the king. Black has gained space and a tempo, but the advanced pawns on d4 and f5 need support now, and White can develop calmly and aim to undermine them.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Ng3.strategy: A more active retreat: the knight eyes f5 and h5 and still covers e4, so Black has to look after the advanced pawns. It stands in front of the g-pawn and can be harassed by an h-pawn advance, so it is a shade worse than the quieter Nf2.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nc5.strategy: Puts the knight on c5, eyeing b7 and e6, but ...e5 at once opens the f8 bishop's attack on it and the knight must run again. White loses more time while Black takes a big centre; fxe5 would lose the knight to ...Bxc5.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6.strategy: Develops and doubles Black's control of e4 and g4, so the retreating knight finds no outpost, and prepares castling. Black keeps its space gains and builds a harmonious set-up around them.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 c5.strategy: Backs the advanced pawn with a pawn at once, so White cannot win it by piling up pieces on d4 and Black's space advantage rests on a solid chain. The price is time: the pieces are still at home and have to be developed behind the pawn wall.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nc6.strategy: Guards d4 with a piece and develops in the same move, so the pawn no longer rests on the queen alone. The knight is tied to the defence of d4 for as long as White keeps up the pressure.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the other knight and attacks the d4 pawn for the first time. The pawn is defended only by the queen, so White makes Black decide how to support its space advantage.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: Challenges the advanced pawn at once. If Black takes and White retakes, the queens face each other on the open d-file and Black can exchange them at the cost of White's castling; if Black holds the pawn, White has a lever against its space advantage.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, whose long diagonal bears on b7 and the centre. It is a slow, solid set-up that ignores the d4 pawn for now and leaves Black to decide how to support its space advantage.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.Nf.strategy: Supports the d4 pawn with a pawn, so Black's space advantage rests on a solid chain rather than on the queen's defence. Black commits to a closed centre in which it has more room and White has to work with pawn breaks to open the game up.

Guards the d4 pawn with a piece and develops: capturing on d4 would lose a knight for a pawn, so the space gain no longer rests on the queen. The knight is tied to the defence of d4 while White keeps up the pressure.

Solid: the pawn guards d5 and f5 and frees the f8-bishop for castling, but it shuts in the c8-bishop and leaves d4 to the queen alone. A second attacker on d4 would force Black to decide how to hold it.

1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.Nf.name: Dunst Opening: Jendrossek Gambit
1.Nc3 d5 2.f4 d4 3.Ne4 f5 4.Nf2 Nf6 5.Nf.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to remove the c5 pawn that holds d4. If Black takes, d4 is again defended only by the queen, but Black is a pawn up and keeps its space; White has to prove that pressure on d4 and quick development are worth the pawn.

Challenges the advanced pawn with a pawn, the standard way to undermine a space advantage: d4 now has two attackers against the c-pawn and the queen. Black can take on e3, when the queens may come off at the cost of White's castling, or let White capture on d4 and open the position.

Adds a second attacker to d4 from the queenside, so Black has to settle the tension. If Black takes on c3, White recaptures with the d-pawn and the queens can come off on the open d-file; the move is sound but less direct than challenging with the e-pawn.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4.strategy: Claims e5 and kingside space at once, with the knight already on c3. It commits the f-pawn early and gives up a calm central set-up, so Black can challenge the pawn at once.

1.Nc3 d6 2.e4.strategy: Claims the centre and turns the game into an ordinary king's-pawn opening with the knight already on its natural square. Black's modest ...d6 has given White a free hand, so White can choose between a broad centre and quick development.

1.Nc3 d6 2.d4.strategy: Builds the other classical centre. The knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, so White cannot add c4 to make it a broad pawn centre, but the pawn gains space, development stays quick and Black has to find a set-up against a strong pawn on d4.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5.strategy: Challenges the f-pawn's claim on e5 head-on. If White takes, Black recaptures and White is left with a half-open f-file; if not, Black keeps a pawn on e5 and has stopped the f-pawn from gaining space.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and aims at the e4 square without committing the e-pawn. Black accepts that White may take space with e4 and f4 together, and counts on counterplay against that broad centre.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and meets the f-pawn from a distance instead of challenging it. Sound, but slower: White gets time to build its centre before Black has made up its mind.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.fxe5.strategy: Takes the challenging pawn and leaves White with a half-open f-file. The exchange costs White the f-pawn's early claim on the centre, so the game turns on whether play along the f-file is worth it.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.d4.strategy: Attacks e5 a second time and recaptures either way: if Black takes on f4 the bishop retakes along the opened diagonal, if Black takes on d4 the queen does. White gets a broad centre and open lines, but Black may gain a tempo against the queen.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.e4.strategy: Offers the f-pawn for open lines and a broad centre: ...exf4 wins a pawn, and White has to prove that its lead in development is worth it. A sharp try that gives Black the easier game if White cannot generate quick pressure.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.fxe5 Nc6.name: Dunst Opening: Hergert Gambit
1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.fxe5 Nc6.strategy: A pawn gambit: Black leaves e5 and develops, and after 4.exd6 Bxd6 is a pawn down but ahead in development, with the bishop already eyeing h2 and White's f-pawn gone. That is enough to be playable, but recapturing at once is the safer way to keep the game level.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.fxe5 dxe5.strategy: The natural recapture: material is level again and Black keeps a pawn in the centre. White is left with a half-open f-file in return for its pawn, while the d-pawn's departure leaves Black's d-file open as well.

1.Nc3 d6 2.f4 e5 3.fxe5 Qh4+.strategy: Gives a check that wins nothing: g3 is the only reply, but it attacks the queen, which has to retreat, so Black loses a tempo and White stays a pawn up. The check is only possible because the f-pawn has left f2.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Attacks e5 at once and forces Black to defend it. The knight goes to its natural square and White keeps every central set-up open.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 straight away and lets Black choose. After the exchange on d4 the queen recaptures and is then hit by a developing move, so White spends a tempo for the open centre, but the extra first move makes up for it.

1.Nc3 e5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares a bishop on the long diagonal, but that diagonal runs through the knight on c3, so the bishop hits nothing until the knight moves. A slow flank move that gives Black time to take the centre.

1.Nc3 e5 2.e3.strategy: A quiet move that opens the king's bishop and prepares a central pawn break, but it makes no claim on the centre at once and lets Black build it freely.

1.Nc3 e5 2.f4.strategy: Offers the f-pawn, but Black takes it and is a clean pawn up. White's only compensation is quick development and a half-open f-file, and with the king's side loosened that is too little.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn that attacks e5 and removes White's central pawn. Black accepts open play and lets White's queen come out to recapture.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a piece and develops, declining to open the centre. White can gain space with d5 at once, driving the knight back, and Black ends up solid but cramped.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and opens the bishop on c8. The structure is solid, but if White trades on e5 and then the queens on d8, Black's king has lost the right to castle and is stuck in the centre.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures at once with the queen, which takes a central post at once. The price is that the queen can be harassed by Black's developing moves.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3.strategy: Overlooks that the pawn on d4 attacks the knight on c3: Black takes it, wins a piece for a pawn, and White's development comes far too late to make up for it.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Nb5.strategy: Attacks the d4 pawn a second time, but Black holds it with ...c5 and then drives the knight on with ...a6. White has lost time and is still a pawn down.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece with a tempo on the queen, which has to move again. Black's knight takes a central square and White's early queen sortie has cost a move.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight and blocks the diagonal from White's queen to the g7 pawn. It does not attack the queen, so Black gains no time, but the position is sound and Black keeps a compact, easy game.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Qf6.strategy: Offers a queen trade, but White does not have to accept: 4.Qc4 hits the loose c7 pawn, and the queen on f6 will be chased by Nd5. Even after 4.Qxf6 Nxf6 5.e4 White has the easier game.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qa4.name: Dunst Opening: Reversed Scandinavian
1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qa4.strategy: Keeps the queen on the board and moves it to the diagonal that eyes the c6 knight. The knight is defended twice, so there is no immediate gain; White gets a flexible, quickly developed game with the queen active.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1.strategy: Retreats the queen to its home square and writes off the sortie. The pawns are level, but White has lost a tempo and Black's knight is already developed, so this is a safe choice for a quiet game with little prospect of an initiative.

1.Nc3 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3+.strategy: Checks and offers to trade queens, so Black must answer at once. The queen is active, but it blocks the c1 bishop and a trade would take the tension out of the game: a forcing way to a level position.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move and accepts that White chooses the type of game. The centre pawn is held, and Black waits to see whether White strikes at it.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.name: Dunst Opening: Billockus-Johansen Gambit
1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, and the sacrifice on f2 does not repair it, since after ...Bxf2+ and Kxf2 Black has given a bishop for a pawn. A gambit that gives away a pawn for too little.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Defends the e5 pawn with the d-pawn, which keeps the centre solid and frees the c8 bishop but cramps the king's bishop. Black gets a sound, rather passive game, and White can challenge the centre at once with more space.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.name: Dunst Opening: Napoleon Attack
1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.background: One of the main lines against 1...e5. Harald Keilhack's 2005 book on the opening says the variation occurs rather often, and Dunst won a quick game with it against Gisela Gresser in New York in 1950.
1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: Attacks e5 a second time with the pawn, so it is attacked twice and defended once. Black has to deal with that at once, and the open lines that follow suit White's quickly developed knights, so White holds the initiative.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.e4.strategy: Puts a pawn in the centre and opens diagonals for the bishops at once. White gives up the fight for e5 in exchange for a straightforward, classical game in which both sides develop freely and neither gets an early edge.

1.Nc3 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d3.strategy: Opens the c1 bishop and guards e4, a modest set-up that does not challenge e5. Black can take the centre with a pawn at once, and White has to play for slow development without the initiative that pressing e5 would keep.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4.strategy: Hits the f5 pawn at once. The knight on c3 already guards e4, so the pawn cannot be won for nothing, and Black has to choose between taking and holding the centre. White gets the lead in the centre either way.

1.Nc3 f5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre with the d-pawn and opens the c1 bishop, with the knight on c3 ready to support an e-pawn advance later. Black's f5 has already loosened the king's side, and White can develop quickly against it.

1.Nc3 f5 2.d3.strategy: Opens the c1 bishop and controls e4, a quiet move that does not touch the f5 pawn. Black can develop in peace and choose its set-up, so White gives up the lead in the centre that the sharper reply would take.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn and wins central material, but the e8-h5 diagonal is already open after ...f5 and stays so. Black has to be ready to give the pawn back or to defend the loosened king's side.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 d6.strategy: Declines the pawn and covers e5, but does nothing against the centre: 3.d4 builds a broad pawn centre at once. Black keeps the loosened king's side and has gained nothing for it, so White is clearly more comfortable.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the e4 pawn, but 3.e5 drives the knight away at once. White gets a pawn wedge in the centre and extra space with a gain of time, and Black's loosened king's side has no compensation.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d3.name: Dunst Opening: Kluever Gambit
1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.d3.strategy: A gambit: White offers a second pawn to open the position for the bishops and the queen. The bishop on d3 would aim along the open diagonal at g6 and the h7 pawn, which makes Black's acceptance risky, but the compensation needs sharp play.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn with a developing move and puts a knight on a central square with the material level. Black's king's side has lost its f-pawn and the diagonal from e8 to h5 is open, so White has the more pleasant game.

1.Nc3 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.f3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open the f-file and the centre. If Black accepts, White has a lead in development after the recapture but is a pawn down with the f-pawn gone from its own king's side, so the gambit needs sharp play to pay off.

1.Nc3 g6 2.h4.name: Dunst Opening: Myers Attack
1.Nc3 g6 2.h4.strategy: A flank advance that threatens h5 to undermine g6, but it costs time and does nothing for development. Black simply develops and meets the threat calmly.

1.Nc3 g6 2.e4.strategy: Takes a pawn to the centre at once, with the knight on c3 already supporting it. Black's plan is to leave the centre to White and attack it later from the flanks and along the long diagonal, so White must keep its pawn centre from becoming a target.

1.Nc3 g6 2.d4.strategy: Takes space with the d-pawn and opens the c1 bishop, keeping the e-pawn advance in reserve. Black's fianchetto then pressures the centre from a distance, and White has to decide how big a pawn centre it wants to build.

1.Nc3 Nf6 2.g4.name: Dunst Opening: Tübingen Gambit
1.Nc3 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Gives away a pawn for nothing: Black takes it with the knight, and when the queen attacks the knight it just retreats. White has weakened the king's side and has no compensation.

1.Nc3 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Claims the centre, with the knight on c3 guarding the pawn, and threatens to drive the f6 knight away with e5. White gets space, and Black has to decide whether to challenge the centre at once or to hold back and attack it later.

1.Nc3 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre without offering the knight on f6 a target, and opens the c1 bishop. The knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, so White builds a compact, flexible game rather than an ambitious pawn centre.
